kicker: Light a lamp in your own house — no need to borrow fire from the neighbours.
summary: AI doesn't only live in the cloud — a good laptop is enough to light your own AI lamp.

quiz.q: Your computer has 16 GB of RAM and you're running AI on it for the first time. Which model should you try first?
options: A 70B model at full size — bigger is smarter
Download lots of models and run them all at once
quiz.explain: An 8B model compressed to 4-bit weighs about 4–5 GB: it fits a 16 GB table and leaves the machine room to breathe. A 32B or 70B model would spill over.

scale.label: The scale
scale.art: Seen from low on the water: an old pine bough reaches across a great moon, a steelyard hanging from it with its beam across the moon's face. The left pan holds a little house with a lit oil lamp; the right, a silver cloud over half a small moon. Six carved stone weights lie half-sunk in the shallows; lift each onto a pan and the beam tips and sways, a paper tag with the reason hangs under the pan, and the water mirrors the whole scale upside down.
scale.prompt: Put each weight on a pan
scale.aria: The scale: run AI on your own machine or in the cloud. Put each weight on the side it favours

sides.name: Lamp at home (local)

sides.name: Lamp in the cloud
sides.aria: The pan for running on the provider's servers

weights.label: Privacy
weights.why: Your questions and documents can stay on your machine.

weights.label: Works offline
weights.why: Download the model once; after that you don't need the internet.

weights.label: No per-use fees
weights.why: You pay with your hardware and electricity, not per token.

weights.label: Top quality
weights.why: The largest models usually live only in the cloud, or need a very powerful machine.

weights.label: Works on weak machines
weights.why: The server does the heavy lifting; your machine just sends and receives text.

weights.label: Always the latest
weights.why: The provider upgrades for you; locally, you download new versions yourself.

scale.weightAria: Put the “{label}” weight on the {side} pan
scale.stonesLabel: Six stone weights in the water: drag one onto a pan, or pick it and use ← → and Enter
scale.wrong: This weight leans the other way.

insight.text: Running AI on your own machine (local AI) can work fully offline once the model is downloaded; in return, the machine must be strong enough.

detail.text: Privacy depends on the tool: Ollama has both models that run on your machine and cloud models (which need an API key). Check before sharing sensitive data.

table.label: A model that fits the table
table.art: A tatami room at night. Behind a long, low tea table, a round window holds a pine bough and the moon; the moonlight throws a bright ellipse on the tabletop — the space still free. The table's length is your computer's RAM; its right quarter always belongs to the tea set (operating system, apps, context). On the wall shelf lie five tied bundles of paper scrolls, each bundle a model. Set one on the table: if it fits, moonlight still lies around it; if it is tight, it covers the moonlight and pushes the tea set; if it is too big, scrolls roll off the edge onto the mat. Slide the table's end board to change the RAM; turn the wooden press to squeeze a model down to the 4-bit version.
table.prompt: Put a model on the table
table.aria: Simulation: put a model on the RAM table to see whether it fits or spills
table.pressAria: The press: squeeze the model down to the 4-bit version (Q4)

states.roomy: Fits — room left for other apps
states.tight: Tight — close some apps, keep questions short
states.spill: Spills over — very slow, or won't run at all

table.modelAria: Put the {label} model ({gb} GB) on a {ram} GB table
table.modelsLabel: Scroll shelf: each bundle is a model, drag or tap it onto the table

rule.text: AI Zen's rule of thumb: the model file should take up less than about half your RAM; the rest is for the system, apps and context.

insight.text: Quantization is like compressing a photo: a 4-bit version is about 3.5 times lighter than 16-bit, at the cost of a little accuracy.

detail.text: Quick estimate: billions of parameters × bits ÷ 8 ≈ GB. For example: 8B at 4.5 bits ≈ 4.5 GB.

table.note: With a separate graphics card, also look at the card's memory (VRAM); Apple Silicon Macs share one pool of RAM between CPU and GPU.

lamps.label: Three lamps
lamps.art: A dark room, one long wooden shelf running away from you. Nearest, a ribbed paper lantern (LM Studio), its candle and wick showing through the paper; midway, an oil lamp with a brass knob to raise its wick (Ollama); at the far end, a bare flame in a glass chimney (llama.cpp) — at first the only light — beside a ceramic oil jar sealed GGUF. Carry fire from the far flame to the nearer lamps: the light and the shadows on the bamboo wall follow your hand. With all three lit, golden threads of oil run from the GGUF jar to every flame.
lamps.aria: Three tools for running AI on your machine: LM Studio, Ollama, llama.cpp
lamps.wickAria: Brass knob that raises the Ollama lamp's wick
lamps.wickHint: The wick is too low to catch — turn the brass knob to raise it, then bring the fire again.
lamps.changeNote: Prices & features change often — check the official site.

lamps.name: LM Studio
lamps.what: Find and download models inside the app (via Hugging Face), chat, attach documents, and switch on a local server for other apps to call.
lamps.fit: Good for beginners who'd rather click than type commands.

fact.text: LM Studio can run fully offline once you have a model; it runs GGUF files through llama.cpp, and MLX on Apple Silicon Macs.

lamps.name: Ollama
lamps.what: One command downloads and runs a model; other apps on your machine call it at localhost:11434.
lamps.fit: Good when you want to connect local AI to apps, workflows and agents.

fact.text: Ollama serves models on your machine at localhost:11434, including an OpenAI-style endpoint that other apps can reuse easily.

lamps.name: llama.cpp
lamps.what: A C/C++ library that runs models right on your machine. The GGUF format was created by the llama.cpp author.
lamps.fit: Good for people who like to fine-tune things by hand; many other apps use it as their engine.

fact.text: llama.cpp is open source (MIT license), runs on CPU, GPU and Apple Silicon, and compresses models from 1.5 to 8 bits.

update.text: In February 2026 the llama.cpp team (ggml) joined Hugging Face; both promised to keep the project open and community-led.

steps.label: Get LM Studio officially
steps.detail: Go to lmstudio.ai and pick the right version for Mac, Windows or Linux.
steps.why: Installers from random places may carry malware.

steps.label: Pick a small model
steps.detail: Search in the app and pick a 4-bit GGUF of about 1–8B; read the model card and license.
steps.why: A model that fits the table runs smoothly; too big and it spills.

steps.label: Download it once
steps.detail: Wait for it to finish; from then on it runs without the internet.
steps.why: The model lives entirely on your machine.

steps.label: Chat, test familiar questions
steps.detail: Ask things you already know the answer to, to see where the model is strong or weak.
steps.why: Know its limits before giving it real work.

lamps.stepsArt: An empty stone footing in a bed of moss under the moon; far off in the mist, your little house, its window still dark. The four parts of a stone lantern lie about — base, shaft, firebox, roof — each carved with one step. Set them in order and the lantern rises; once the roof is on, the firebox lights, and so does the window of the house far away.
lamps.wrongHint: Not this step yet — a lamp needs the right order.

insight.text: All three lamps burn the same oil: LM Studio, Ollama and llama.cpp can all run GGUF model files from Hugging Face.

lamps.detail: Prices & features change often — always check the official site before installing.

scroll.label: The command scroll
scroll.art: A close view of a tokonoma alcove: a hanging calligraphy scroll, its heavy lower rod with a tassel. A small oil lamp on the floor lights it from below, so the scroll's soft shadow falls on the plaster above it; beside it, a ceramic vase with one flowering branch. Pull the rod down and the paper unrolls section by section, each a command with a small note in the margin, like a teacher's advice to a student.
scroll.aria: Code scroll: four basic Ollama commands, with notes beside them
scroll.rodAria: The scroll's lower rod: pull it down (or ↓, Enter) to unroll one section at a time

code.code:
ollama pull gemma4:e2b
ollama run gemma4:e2b
ollama list
curl http://localhost:11434/api/chat -d '{"model": "gemma4:e2b", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}], "stream": false}'

notes.text: Downloads the model to your machine. Only this step needs the internet; this sample model is about 7 GB.
Opens a chat right in the terminal. Type /bye to leave.
Lists the models stored on your machine.
Other apps call the model through the local port — no API key needed.

scroll.modelNote: The model name comes from an example in the Ollama docs and will change over time; look up current names in the Ollama library before running.

insight.text: With Ollama, “ollama run” both downloads a model and opens a chat right on your machine.

detail.text: Local models called via localhost need no API key; Ollama's cloud models do need a key and send your data out.

circle.label: Four stones by the pond
circle.art: The camera skims a round pond under the moon: the pond becomes a thin ellipse, the moon's reflection a long broken road running toward you. Four stones sit round it — two small on the far bank, two large on the near one — each keeping a small paper lamp. Touch a stone and its lamp lights, its warm streak stretching across the water toward you; hear all four and the streaks and the moon's road gather at the pond's centre.
circle.aria: Circle of views: should creative and marketing people run AI locally or in the cloud?

view.text: Contracts, phone numbers, client files: run it locally so the data never goes to anyone else's server.

stones.who: The one who needs top quality

view.text: Important drafts, hard tasks: big cloud models are usually still better than any model that fits a laptop.
Heavy daily use: local saves per-use fees. Light use: a cloud plan can be cheaper than buying a new machine.
Running a small model yourself shows you first-hand: AI is a file, with a size, a speed and limits.

common.text: They agree: no choice is right for every task. What differs is how sensitive the data is, the quality needed, and the budget.

insight.text: Many people use both: sensitive work runs locally, work that needs the very best goes to the cloud — choosing deliberately each time.
